message.content:
**Answer**

The last common ancestor of a lion (*Panthera leo*) and a zebra (*Equus quagga*) is the most recent common ancestor of the two orders **Carnivora** (the lion’s order) and **Perissodactyla** (the zebra’s order). Both of those orders belong to the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**, which is one of the major groups of placental mammals.

- **Timeframe** – The split between Carnivora and Perissodactyla is estimated to have occurred roughly **70–80 million years ago** (late Cretaceous to early Paleogene).  
- **Nature of the ancestor** – This ancestor would have been a small, likely insectivorous or omnivorous mammal that lived on the ancient supercontinent Laurasia. It possessed the basic mammalian body plan but had not yet evolved the specialized features that later gave rise to the diverse carnivores (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) or the odd‑toed ungulates (horses, rhinos, tapirs, zebras, etc.).

So, in short: the common ancestor of lion and zebra is a **Laurasiatherian mammal that lived about 70–80 million years ago**, predating the divergence of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the superorders Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria clade. That ancestor would have lived around 70-80 million years ago. So the answer: the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is a Laurasiatherian mammal that lived about 70-80 million years ago, before the divergence of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. Alternatively, the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria) lived about 100-120 million years ago. But the more specific answer: the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a member of the Laurasiatheria clade. So we can say: the last common ancestor of lion and zebra was a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous or early Paleogene, part of the Laurasiatheria group. We can mention that the divergence occurred around 70-80 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
